# Spelled-out small numbers, with a numeral fallback. A fixed word vector indexed by `n + 1`
# reads fine and renders "NA" the day the count exceeds it — silently, since `cat` is happy to
# print NA.
num_word <- function(n) {
  w <- c("Zero", "One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five", "Six", "Seven", "Eight", "Nine", "Ten")
  if (n >= 0 && n < length(w)) w[n + 1L] else format(n)
}

**Where are British Columbia's floodplains, and what is happening to them?** This repo answers
that one watershed group at a time: it maps the valley bottom a salmon-bearing river can flood,
then measures how the land cover inside it changed between 2017 and 2023 and tries to say why.

It is a **tool for finding where to look**. Nothing here has been checked on the ground — read
[Reading the outputs](#reading-the-outputs-experimental) before you use a number from it.

```{r fig-floodplain, echo=FALSE, fig.alt=paste0("Two panels. Left: the ", FIG_AREA_LABEL, " watershed group, its ", FIG_SPECIES_LABEL, "-accessible stream network, and the modelled ", fp_scen_short(FIG_PRIMARY), " floodplain drawn as a dark ribbon along the valleys, with a red box marking a detail window. Right: that window at ", tolower(num_word(nrow(s_run))), " flood-factor scenarios nested inside one another - ", paste(sprintf("%s %s", fp_scen_short(s_run$scenario_id), tolower(s_run$description)), collapse = ", "), ".")}
knitr::include_graphics(fp_fig_require("floodplain.png"))
```

## What it does

For an area — a watershed group, optionally a single reach — the pipeline runs three steps:

1. **Network.** Pull the stream a species can actually reach, via
   [`link`](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/link). See
   [What "accessible" means](#what-accessible-means): it is a connectivity model, **not** modelled
   spawning or rearing habitat.
2. **Floodplain.** Delineate the valley bottom around that network with the Valley Confinement
   Algorithm, via [`flooded`](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/flooded), on the national
   30 m DEM.
3. **Land-cover change.** Classify 10 m Impact Observatory land cover for 2017, 2020 and 2023,
   find the patches that changed, and tag each one against overlay layers — fire, harvest — via
   [`drift`](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/drift).

The **method lives in the packages**. This repo is the thin driver: config per area, one runner,
and a provenance record of what produced each output.

## Reading the outputs (experimental)

**This is a screening tool, not a validated change-detection product.** The floodplain is
modelled from a DEM. The land cover is a global product applied to BC valley bottoms. Neither has
been field-validated. Treat every patch as a *candidate* — somewhere worth looking — rather than
a measurement.

Used that way it works: the model surfaces real riparian change in the Bulkley that would
otherwise have to be found by eye, at a scale no one is going to walk.

```{r fig-attribution, echo=FALSE, fig.alt=paste0("Top: the ", FIG_AREA_LABEL, " watershed group with every modelled floodplain tree-loss patch ", FIG_SPAN[1], "-", FIG_SPAN[2], " drawn as a dot sized by area and coloured by attributed cause - ", paste(sprintf("%s in %s", src, fp_cause_colour(src)), collapse = ", "), ", and ", fp_cause_colour(UNATTRIBUTED), " where nothing yet attributes it. Bottom: a stacked bar of the same loss by area, showing those sources accounting for roughly a third of it between them.")}
knitr::include_graphics(fp_fig_require("attribution.png"))
```

**Attribution is the part that is growing.** Each change patch is intersected with the overlay
layers named in `config/disturbance.yml` and tagged with what it hits. Fire and harvest are what
that file lists today, and between them they source about a third of the tree loss above — a
third that used to sit undifferentiated. The framework is layer-agnostic: **any spatial layer we
can get is a config line**, not a code change. Confirmed riparian clearing for agriculture,
forest health, tenure — each is one entry away. A patch can carry several tags at once, which is
the honest answer for salvage logging after a fire.

What we still do not know:

- **The rest of the tree loss has no source yet.** Some of it is real removal we cannot tie to a
  layer; some is drought or seasonal drying, water-level change, terrain shadow or plain
  misclassification. Those have not been separated from one another, so the residual is a work
  list, not a measurement.
- **"Tree loss" is a class transition, not confirmed forest removal.** What is measured is pixels
  leaving the tree class.
- **Acquisition timing is unknown and unrecoverable.** `io-lulc-annual-v02` items are one
  composite per zone per year and carry no acquisition date and no `created` or `updated`
  property. A wet year against a dry one could skew a figure and we cannot quantify that.
- **Groups are not comparable to each other yet.** With no treed-area denominator (#38), a group
  whose floodplain is mostly open water cannot be set against a forested one on hectares lost.
- **No patch-level field QA has been done** (#27).
- **The floodplain is modelled too** — VCA output on a 30 m DEM, against the *accessible* network.
  Despite the `ff` scenario names it is **not** a flood-frequency product.

Everything is published openly so it can be interrogated. **Please do**, and file what you find.

## What "accessible" means

The network we delineate against is the **accessible** network: stream connected to the ocean
without an intervening natural barrier, below a per-species gradient ceiling. It is a
*connectivity* model, not modelled spawning or rearing habitat — which bcfishpass also produces
and which is far more restrictive.

The ceiling is per species. These values are **copied** from link's config bundle at
`extdata/configs/bcfishpass/parameters_fresh.csv`, column `access_gradient_max` — verified
against link 0.50.0 on 2026-09-04. They can move with a link release and nothing here would
notice, so re-check them when link is upgraded:

| species | `access_gradient_max` |
|---|---|
| CH, CM, **CO**, PK, SK | **0.15** |
| ST, WCT | 0.20 |
| **BT**, CT, DV, RB | **0.25** |

So a chinook or coho area is delineated against stream up to **15%** gradient and a bull trout
area up to **25%**. That is why bull trout shows more accessible km than chinook in the same
group, and why coho and chinook networks are *identical* wherever both are modelled.

**The gap between accessible and modelled habitat is large**, so the distinction is not academic.
Measured 2026-09-03 at order ≥ 3:

| WSG | species | accessible km | spawning km | rearing km | spawning as % of accessible |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FRAN | ch | 2139 | 587 | 803 | **27%** |
| BOWR | ch | 1017 | 649 | 736 | 64% |
| LNTH | ch | 694 | 448 | 509 | 65% |
| KOTL | bt | 1921 | 921 | 1636 | 48% |
| PCEA | bt | 2194 | 888 | 1743 | 40% |

Read a published area as *"floodplain along stream this species can reach"*, never as *"floodplain
along spawning habitat"*.

Which config bundle produced a network is **recorded, not assumed** — `fresh.log.config_name`
carries it per group and step 1 resolves it into `provenance.json`. The `bcfishpass` bundle opts
subsurface flow in as a barrier; the `default` bundle leaves it out, and the two disagree by about
0.7% province-wide.

## What a flood factor is

`ff0N` is a **scenario**, not a return period. Each one widens the same delineation to a
different ecological extent. Every area carries its own `config/<area>/flood_scenarios.csv`;
this table is read from `` `r area_dir` ``, the group the figures above come from:

```{r scenarios, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    scenario = s$scenario_id,
    `flood factor` = s$flood_factor,
    extent = s$description,
    `run by default` = ifelse(s$run == "TRUE" | s$run == TRUE, "yes", "no"),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r scenarios-run, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
# "Three are modelled by default" was written under the table that generates itself, which is
# the recurrence shape #77 exists to remove — a fourth `run = TRUE` row would move the table and
# leave the sentence wrong with nothing to notice. Count it from the same frame the table came
# from.
n_run <- sum(s$run == "TRUE" | s$run == TRUE)
cat(num_word(n_run),
    " of these are modelled by default; the rest are configured and off. ",
    "Turning one on is a `run` column edit, not a code change.\n", sep = "")
```

## Design

- **One codebase, config per area.** Code is single-source in `scripts/`; the per-area bits live
  in `config/<area>/`. Adding an area is adding a directory, not a code change.
- **Several species coexist in one area.** Outputs are keyed by species (`streams_co3`,
  `co_ff04` / `ch_ff06`), so MORR carries both coho and chinook without either overwriting the
  other.
- **Regions batch a set of groups.** `config/regions/<region>.yml` names the groups and a species
  preference. A region run **reconciles** each area's config rather than regenerating it, so a
  second species' scenario rows, citations and every comment survive. `DRY=1` writes nothing at
  all.
- **A floodplain can be attributed per watercourse.** Optional `attribute_by:` adds one row per
  watercourse, so a delineation answers "where is the floodplain of *this* river". Rows **overlap**
  where ground is genuinely shared at a confluence — on MORR that is 43.6% of the floodplain, so a
  hard partition would mis-assign nearly half of it. A companion `patch_watercourse_*` table
  carries two fractions, and only one of them adds up: `overlap_frac` describes coverage,
  `apportion_weight` sums to 1 and is the one to aggregate with.
- **Every published layer carries the item key** — `wsg`, `species`, `scenario` — so many areas
  can merge into one GeoPackage and stay separable by attribute.
- **Parity fixture.** `config/neexdzii/` must reproduce known-good numbers — coho-3 network
  **673.5 km**, floodplain `co_ff04` **142.8 km²**, tree loss **770.0 ha** — before any change is
  trusted. Re-baselined 2026-09-01 under `flooded` 0.5.0. The previous contract
  (678.2 / 171.0 / 943.13) is **dead, not superseded**: it came from a bankfull regression fed
  hectares where Hall et al. specify km² and mm where they specify cm/yr. Record these as a fresh
  contract, never as a delta from the old.
- **Rebuilds are byte-reproducible.** GDAL stamps every GeoPackage with the wall-clock time of
  the write, which would make each rebuild a new checksum regardless of content. The stamp is
  pinned to a fixed epoch (`scripts/fp_gpkg.R`) and
  `scripts/floodplain_lcc/gpkg_determinism-check.R` asserts it. One stated limit: rewriting a
  single layer into an *existing* GeoPackage is not byte-stable, because SQLite records write
  history in its header.

## Where it has been run

Read from `config/regions/*.yml`, which is what the region runner itself consumes:

```{r roster, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(fp_readme_roster(), row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("region", "species preference", "watershed groups"))
```

Plus the `neexdzii` parity fixture, which is a reach inside BULK and is deliberately not part of
any region. The species column is the region's **preference**: the runner takes the first one
actually modelled in a group at the configured order, so a group could in principle resolve to
the second entry.

This is **what is configured**, which is not the same as what has been modelled, published, or
re-run at the current model version — MCGR and PINE are published but cannot be re-run as things
stand (#76). For what is actually available to download, ask the catalogue rather than this page.

## Running it

```bash
Rscript scripts/run_area.R <area> [steps]     # steps default to 1,2,3
Rscript scripts/run_region.R <region>         # every group in a region, resumable
```

Run a non-default species with environment overrides rather than a config edit:
`FP_SPECIES=ch FP_PRIMARY_SCENARIO=ch_ff06 Rscript scripts/run_area.R <area>`.

Prerequisites: a local `fwapg` PostgreSQL (standard libpq environment variables);
`link` ≥ 0.44.0, `flooded`, `drift` ≥ 0.6.0, `fresh`, `terra` ≥ 1.8-10 (see `scripts/packages.R`);
internet for the national MRDEM-30 DEM and the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC; and the
disturbance overlay layers loaded into `fwapg` via `bcdata bc2pg`.

Long runs want `caffeinate -s` in front of them — macOS idle sleep kills a detached job, and the
region runner is resumable so an interrupted group picks up where it stopped.

## Run provenance

Every run writes `data/<area>/provenance.json` recording **what produced the outputs**: the link
log row for the network, the VCA parameters and DEM geometry for the floodplain, and a content
digest of the classified rasters for the land cover.

Each section splits into `inputs` (a function of the inputs, byte-stable across reruns, summarised
as one `inputs_hash`) and `outputs` (a digest of what came out). Two questions, two answers:
*same ingredients?* and *same result?* — and the second is deliberately not folded into the first,
because "same answer from different data" is worth knowing separately from "different answer".

The land-cover fingerprint is a digest of the **classified rasters**, not the STAC item ids: an
io-lulc item id is `<tile>-<year>` and the items carry no `created` or `updated`, so an upstream
reprocess in place leaves every id identical.

```bash
Rscript scripts/floodplain_lcc/provenance-check.R <area>   # no database needed
```

## Publishing

Modelling and publishing are separate repos and the dependency points **one way**:
[`stac_floodplains_bc`](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/stac_floodplains_bc) reads this
repo's `data/` and publishes it. This repo knows nothing about it beyond the reminder a run
prints. What the catalogue holds, how to query it, and how to download from it are documented
there — including the collection id, which is **hyphenated** and is not the repository name.

## Method

The valley confinement approach, the flood-factor scenarios and their ecological framing come
from the literature the scenario config cites:

- Nagel, D.E., J.M. Buffington, S.L. Parkes, S. Wenger and J.R. Goode. 2014.
  *A landscape scale valley confinement algorithm: delineating unconfined valley bottoms for
  geomorphic, aquatic, and riparian applications.* USDA Forest Service General Technical Report
  RMRS-GTR-321 — <https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/45516>
- Hall, J.E., D.M. Holzer and T.J. Beechie. 2007. *Predicting river floodplain and lateral channel
  migration for salmon habitat conservation.* Journal of the American Water Resources Association
  43(3):786–797 — <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1752-1688.2007.00063.x>
- Opperman, J.J., R. Luster, B.A. McKenney, M. Roberts and A.W. Meadows. 2010. *Ecologically
  functional floodplains: connectivity, flow regime, and scale.* Journal of the American Water
  Resources Association 46(2):211–226 — <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1752-1688.2010.00426.x>

```{r citekeys, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
# A count rather than a 12-item dump of Zotero keys: it regenerates from the config the way the
# rest of this page's facts do, and the keys themselves are one file away.
#
# `n - 3` would be one fact derived twice — it assumes the three written out above are all still
# in the CSV, and goes quietly wrong the day one is not. Take the difference instead, and let
# the render fail loudly if a named key stops being there.
named <- c("nagel_etal2014LandscapeScale", "hall_etal2007Predictingriver",
           "opperman_etal2010EcologicallyFunctional")
keys <- fp_readme_citekeys()
if (!all(named %in% keys)) {
  stop("a citation written out in the Method section is no longer in flood_scenarios.csv: ",
       paste(setdiff(named, keys), collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE)
}
# "Those three" was a second copy of `length(named)` — round 2's fix reappearing 138 lines down.
cat("Those ", tolower(num_word(length(named))), " and ", length(setdiff(keys, named)),
    " more sit in the `citations` column of `config/", FIG_AREA,
    "/flood_scenarios.csv`, one set per scenario.\n", sep = "")
```

## Licence

The **code** in this repository is
[MIT](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/floodplains/blob/main/LICENSE).

The two figures are the only derived data this repo redistributes, and they carry obligations
from their inputs: land cover from Impact Observatory's `io-lulc-annual-v02`
([CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)), **modified** by clipping to modelled
floodplain extents and cross-tabulating 2017 against 2023; terrain containing information licensed
under the Open Government Licence – Canada (MRDEM-30, Natural Resources Canada); and stream
network containing information licensed under the Open Government Licence – British Columbia
(Freshwater Atlas, Province of British Columbia).

The **published products** are a different question with a different answer, and it is documented
where they live — see
[`stac_floodplains_bc/ATTRIBUTION.md`](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/stac_floodplains_bc/blob/main/ATTRIBUTION.md).
